analysis.overview: vLLM 是目前开源大语言模型（LLM）推理与服务领域的「事实标准」引擎。它最初由 UC Berkeley Sky Computing Lab 开发，核心创新是利用 PagedAttention 技术解决 LLM 服务中的 KV Cache 内存碎片问题，从而实现极高的吞吐量。该项目目前处于高速发展和高度成熟的阶段，生态位类似于推理界的 PyTorch，不仅支持海量模型（如最新的 DeepSeek V4、GLM-5.3），还向下兼容极其丰富的硬件后端（CUDA、ROCm、CPU、XPU、TPU 等）。对于企业级部署和 AI 应用开发者而言，vLLM 是首选的底层推理基座。虽然竞争对手有 TensorRT-LLM 和 TGI，但 vLLM 凭借极佳的易用性、极快的社区响应速度（对新模型的支持通常在几天内完成）以及活跃的开源生态占据主导地位。
what_it_does: 核心内存管理：通过 PagedAttention 高效管理 KV Cache，减少内存浪费（对应 `csrc/cache.h` 和 `vllm/core`）。
连续批处理（Continuous Batching）：在请求级别动态调度 prefill 和 decode 阶段，最大化 GPU 利用率（对应 `vllm/engine`）。
高性能算子与融合：包含大量针对不同精度（FP8, INT4, AWQ, Marlin）优化的自定义 CUDA/C++ 算子（对应 `csrc/libtorch_stable` 和 `csrc/attention`）。
多硬件后端支持：除了 NVIDIA GPU，还原生支持 AMD ROCm、Intel XPU 以及纯 CPU/Mac 运行（对应 `csrc/cpu` 和 `cmake/`）。
OpenAI 兼容 API 服务：提供开箱即用的高并发 API 服务器，支持流式输出（对应 `vllm/entrypoints/openai`）。
结构化输出与工具调用：支持基于 xgrammar 的结构化生成和复杂的 Tool Calling 解析（对应 `vllm/tool_parsers` 和 `vllm/parser`）。
投机解码（Speculative Decoding）：支持 n-gram、EAGLE 等多种投机解码算法以加速推理（对应 `vllm/spec_decode`）。
stack: C++20 / CUDA 20 / HIP 20
Rust (用于高性能 Frontend/Router)
PyTorch (锁定 2.13.0)
构建系统: CMake, Ninja, setuptools, setuptools-rust
环境管理: uv (强制要求)
CI/CD: Buildkite (重型 GPU 测试), GitHub Actions

architecture.role: 核心调度器
architecture.notes: 负责 Continuous Batching 和请求生命周期管理。纯 Python 逻辑，不依赖 GPU 即可进行逻辑测试。

architecture.role: 模型执行与并行控制
architecture.notes: 处理张量并行(TP)、流水线并行(PP)和模型权重的加载。近期热点，常用于适配新模型架构。

architecture.role: CUDA 核心算子库
architecture.notes: 包含 PagedAttention、Marlin、AWQ、MoE 等极度优化的 CUDA Kernel。代码量大，是性能优化的主战场。

architecture.role: CPU 后端算子库
architecture.notes: 包含 ARM NEON/x86 AVX 优化的 C++ 算子。对于无 GPU 的 Mac 开发者，这是最核心的切入点。

architecture.role: 高性能路由与前端
architecture.notes: 近期提交热点（21个 commit）。项目正在将部分 Python 层的 API 路由和解析逻辑下沉到 Rust 以降低开销。

architecture.role: API 服务入口
architecture.notes: 实现 OpenAI 兼容接口、gRPC 接口。近期活跃于 Tool Calling 严格模式的控制。

architecture.role: 工具调用解析器
architecture.notes: 处理各类模型（如 DeepSeek V4, GLM）的特定 Tool Calling 模板解析。

architecture.role: 性能基准测试
architecture.notes: 包含端到端吞吐量、延迟以及 Kernel 级别的微基准测试（如 `benchmarks/kernels`）。

analysis.data_flow:
一次推理请求的数据流如下：
1. 请求通过 `vllm/entrypoints`（如 OpenAI API 服务器）进入系统，经过 Rust 前端或 Python 解析器进行格式校验和 Tokenization。
2. 解析后的请求被送入 `vllm/engine`（通常是 AsyncLLMEngine）。引擎的 Scheduler 会根据当前的 KV Cache 碎片情况（PagedAttention 逻辑）决定是否分配物理块，并将请求加入 Continuous Batching 队列。
3. 引擎将 Batch 好的请求元数据（Input Tokens, Block Tables）派发给 `vllm/model_executor`。
4. Executor 调用底层的 PyTorch 模型代码，在执行 Attention 和特定算子（如 MoE、Quantization）时，通过 PyTorch C++ Extension 桥接调用 `csrc/` 下的自定义 Kernel（如 `csrc/libtorch_stable` 中的 CUDA 算子，或 `csrc/cpu` 中的 CPU 算子）。
5. 前向传播完成后，Logits 被送入采样器（Sampler）生成下一个 Token。
6. 新生成的 Token 被更新回引擎状态，并通过异步队列流式（Streaming）返回给 `entrypoints`，最终推送到客户端。整个过程循环直至遇到 EOS 或达到最大长度。

hotspots.why: 最近有 21 个 commit。项目正在进行架构演进，将高频的 API 路由、请求校验和部分调度逻辑从 Python 迁移到 Rust，以突破 Python GIL 带来的并发瓶颈。
最近有 8 个 commit。主要在完善 API 服务器的功能，例如增加 `--tool-strict-level` 来控制结构化标签的激活，提升企业级服务的稳定性。
合计 8 个 commit。为了支持最新发布的模型（如 DeepSeek V4），正在密集修复和添加特定模型的解析逻辑（如缺失 `string=` 的解析修复）。
最近有 4 个 commit。主要在适配新模型（如 GLM-5.3-Flash、DeepSeek V4）的执行逻辑，以及处理 KV Cache 组之间的映射共享优化。

hotspots.path: csrc/libtorch_stable (隐含于 ROCm/KV Cache 修复)
hotspots.why: 底层 Kernel 持续优化中。例如 GLM-5.3 的 Cooperative top-k 优化、ROCm 平台的 KV Offload 修复、DSv4.1 的 NaN 分数处理等。

analysis.build_and_test:
在没有 GPU 的 Apple Silicon Mac 上运行和测试：
1. 环境准备：根据 `AGENTS.md`，必须使用 `uv`。执行 `uv venv --python 3.12` 并 `source .venv/bin/activate`。
2. 绕过 GPU 限制：`setup.py` 中已包含逻辑 `if sys.platform.startswith("darwin") ... VLLM_TARGET_DEVICE = "cpu"`。因此在 Mac 上编译会自动回退到 CPU 后端。
3. 编译安装：执行 `VLLM_TARGET_DEVICE=cpu uv pip install -e .`。这会调用 CMake 编译 `csrc/cpu` 下的 C++ 代码（如 ARM NEON 优化的 Attention）。
4. 运行测试：安装 CPU 测试依赖 `uv pip install -r requirements/test/cpu.txt`（或 `common.txt`）。
5. 测试命令：使用 `pytest tests/basic_correctness/ -v`。注意：必须避开 `tests/cuda/` 和 `tests/rocm/` 目录，专注于 `tests/engine/`、`tests/parser/` 等纯逻辑测试或 CPU Kernel 测试。
analysis.maintainers: 维护节奏极快，属于高频发版（8月发布 v0.27.1 和 v0.28.0，9月发布 v0.29.0）。社区由 UC Berkeley 创始团队及各大厂（NVIDIA, AMD, 阿里等）的核心开发者共同维护。Review 风格极其严格：根据 `AGENTS.md`，项目实行 Fail-closed 策略，严禁提交无意义的刷 KPI PR（如单纯改拼写），严禁纯 AI 生成的代码，要求提交者必须对代码有端到端的理解并附带详细的测试/Benchmark 结果。社区入口主要在 Slack (`slack.vllm.ai`) 和 GitHub Issues。
gaps: CPU 后端算子滞后：`csrc/cpu` 存在，但对新模型（如 DeepSeek V4 MLA、FP8 MoE）的支持远落后于 CUDA 后端。候选人可以在 Mac 上用 C++/ARM NEON 实现这些前沿算子的 CPU 版本。
CPU 性能基线缺失：`benchmarks/kernels/cpu` 目录下的微基准测试脚本远少于 CUDA。缺乏系统的 CPU 推理性能追踪。
调度器（Engine）的纯逻辑单元测试不足：很多调度逻辑的测试依然隐式依赖完整的模型加载，导致在无 GPU 环境下难以快速跑通。需要更多的 Mock 测试。
Rust-Python 边界测试薄弱：`rust/src` 正在大量重构，跨 FFI 边界的异常处理和内存泄漏测试在 Mac 上完全可以进行，目前这块覆盖率有待提升。
文档中缺乏非 NVIDIA 硬件的 Kernel 开发指南：如何为 CPU 或 XPU 添加新算子的文档极少，导致社区贡献门槛高。
analysis.ownership_target: 建议长期负责 **CPU 后端算子（`csrc/cpu`）与 Engine 调度逻辑**。作为资深 GPU Kernel 工程师，你对 CUDA、Triton 和内存排布（如 MLA、MoE 结构）有极深的理解。在只有 Mac 的硬约束下，你可以将最新的 CUDA 算子逻辑（如 DeepSeek V4 的 MLA 或 FP8 算子）降级/移植为高质量的 C++ ARM NEON 实现。这不仅能让 vLLM 在端侧/Mac 上的本地开发体验大幅提升，还能向 Maintainer 证明你对前沿模型底层架构的深刻理解。同时，参与纯 Python 的 `vllm/engine` 调度优化（如 Continuous Batching 策略）完全不需要 GPU。通向 Maintainer 的路径是：先通过高难度的 CPU 算子移植建立技术威望，随后在 Slack 中参与核心架构讨论，最后利用 Colab T4 提交/Review 关键的 CUDA 性能优化 PR。

phase_30: 安装 `uv`，在 Mac 上配置 Python 3.12 虚拟环境。
阅读 `AGENTS.md` 和 `CONTRIBUTING.md`，了解严格的提交流程。
通过 `VLLM_TARGET_DEVICE=cpu uv pip install -e .` 在 Mac 上成功编译项目。
阅读 `csrc/cpu/cpu_attn.cpp` 和 `vllm/engine/async_llm_engine.py`，理解 CPU 算子桥接和调度流程。
运行 `pytest tests/engine/`，修复一个简单的纯逻辑 Bug 或补充一个缺失的 CPU 单元测试，提交第一个 PR。
phase_60: 挑选一个近期热门但 CPU 尚未支持的特性（例如某种特定的 FP8 量化格式或 MoE 算子，参考 `csrc/libtorch_stable` 中的最新提交）。
在 `csrc/cpu` 中用 C++ 实现该算子的 CPU Fallback 版本。
在 `benchmarks/kernels/cpu` 中添加对应的性能测试脚本，并在 Mac 上完成 Benchmark。
在 Colab T4 上短暂运行，确保你的改动没有破坏 CUDA 侧的编译和基础逻辑。
提交 PR，并在描述中详细对比 CPU 侧的性能提升，明确说明这是为了增强本地开发和端侧部署能力。
phase_90: 深入 `vllm/engine`，寻找 Continuous Batching 或 Chunked Prefill 中的调度瓶颈，提出纯逻辑层的优化方案。
加入 `slack.vllm.ai`，在 #development 频道分享你对 CPU 后端架构的重构建议或调度器优化思路。
开始 Review 其他社区成员提交的关于模型执行 (`vllm/model_executor`) 和算子融合的 PR，利用你的 GPU 经验指出潜在的显存碎片或同步开销问题。
在积累 5 个以上高质量 PR 后，向核心团队申请特定模块（如 `csrc/cpu` 或 `vllm/engine`）的 Triage / Reviewer 权限。

risks: 风险：项目高度以 GPU 为中心，纯 CPU/Mac 的 PR 可能会被核心团队忽视或优先级排得很低。对策：在 PR 描述中强调该改动对「降低社区贡献门槛」和「本地 Debug 体验」的巨大价值，并在 Slack 中主动 @ 相关模块的负责人（如负责 CPU/XPU 后端的 Intel/Apple 贡献者）。
风险：Rust 前端重构导致底层 C++ 接口频繁变动，维护 Mac 编译分支成本高。对策：熟练使用 `uv` 进行增量编译，保持与 `main` 分支的高频 Rebase。
风险：缺乏高端 GPU 导致无法验证复杂的分布式训练/推理性能 Bug。对策：扬长避短，坚决不碰需要多卡 NCCL 验证的 PR，专注于单卡 Kernel 逻辑（用 Colab T4 验证）和纯 CPU 调度逻辑。

issues.title: [Bug]: NIXL HMA receive failures can return HTTP 200 with corrupted tokens
issues.body:
### Your current environment

<details>
<summary>Reproduction environment</summary>

```text
Hardware: 2x NVIDIA B200 (one prefill, one decode)
Model: RedHatAI/gemma-4-26B-A4B-it-FP8-dynamic
Topology: disaggregated prefill/decode, NIXL HMA, TP1 per role
NIXL: 1.3.2
Decode --block-size: 64
Prefill --block-size: 128
KV load failure policy: fail
Routing: EPP always-disaggregated profile
```

Affected builds observed:

- Red Hat AI 3.5 RC1: `vllm-0.24.0+rhaiv.2-b642109f`
- Upstream main `71b0da7c4ecca10a9f11f535fc370cf988ce12d7`:
  `vllm-0.27.2rc1.dev64+g71b0da7c4`

The Red Hat build is based on the v0.24 line. The fail-closed fix also applies
cleanly to upstream tag `v0.24.0` (`ee0da84ab9`).

</details>

### 🐛 Describe the bug

When a NIXL KV receive fails for an HMA model, the request can continue decoding
from invalid/uninitialized KV and return an apparently successful HTTP 200
response containing corrupted tokens.

This is separate from whether a given heterogeneous block-size layout should be
supported. Unsupported layouts may legitimately fail their compatibility or
runtime handshake, but that failure must not allow token generation.

#### Reproduction

Run Gemma-4-26B FP8 in disaggregated prefill/decode mode with `NixlConnector`,
prefill block size 128, and decode block size 64. Route a request through both
roles:

```bash
curl http://<endpoint>/v1/chat/completions \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{
    "model": "gemma-4-26b-a4b-fp8",
    "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "What is Kubernetes?"}],
    "max_tokens": 64
  }'
```

The decode log shows that compatibility hashing passes, then runtime handshake
setup rejects the effective HMA block geometry:

```text
NIXL compatibility check passed
AssertionError: Local block size 32 is not divisible by remote block size 64 or vice versa.
NIXL transfer failure: handshake_failed
Skipping KV post-processing for failed request <request-id>
POST /v1/chat/completions HTTP/1.1 200 OK
KV Transfer metrics: Num successful transfers=0
```

The API nevertheless returns 64 tokens of gibberish with
`"finish_reason":"length"`.

#### Expected behavior

Any unrecoverable HMA receive/handshake failure must fail the request before a
sampled token is consumed or returned. The client should receive an error and
no generated content.

#### Cause

Uniform-cache receive failures are propagated through `invalid_block_ids`.
HMA block IDs are scoped to independent KV pools, so NIXL intentionally omits
them because the flat IDs cannot identify the failed group safely. The request
is still reported as finished receiving, leaving the scheduler without a
failure signal and allowing decode to proceed.

#### Related work

- #42895 tracks support for heterogeneous physical block sizes, not fail-closed
  handling after a rejected handshake.
- #47812 discusses group-aware recovery for hybrid caches.
- #40364 added block-level handshake-failure recovery for uniform caches and
  left HMA handling as a TODO.
- #52232 propagates unrecoverable HMA receive failures by request ID and proves
  the same reproduction returns HTTP 500 with no choices, content, usage, or
  generated tokens.

### Before submitting a new issue...

- [x] I searched existing and past issues. The related issues above do not
  track the fail-open corrupted-output behavior.

issues.title: [RFC]: Stateless Responses API in the Rust frontend
issues.body:
## Motivation.

Add native Responses API support to the Rust frontend so clients can use its serving pipeline without a Python API-server fallback. The API must preserve structured conversation input and produce consistent Responses objects whether the client requests buffered JSON or streaming events.

> [!NOTE]
> This RFC follows up on the **non-stateful Responses API** item under "Additional APIs" in the [June 2026 Rust Frontend Feature Parity roadmap (#44280)](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/44280). The item was marked 🧭 for a design discussion before implementation, covering the intended API/architecture, engine co-design if needed, and testing plan.

This proposal defines a useful first subset, its ownership boundaries and its validation plan. It reuses existing inference infrastructure rather than porting every Python Responses feature or adding an agent runtime.

## Proposed Change.

### 1. Design principles

1. **Self-contained requests, no server-owned conversation state.** Clients supply the complete relevant history. The frontend retains no response objects or conversation history for later requests and introduces no future storage scaffolding.
2. **Shared execution, API-specific ownership.** Reuse rendering, media processing, tokenization, parsing and engine access. Responses owns input conversion, its public items and events, and its output lifecycle.
3. **Explicit acceptance and compatibility choices.** Reject unsupported options that change behavior. Document deliberate compatibility exceptions and their costs.
4. **Validation proportional to distinct risk.** Check protocol invariants with deterministic CPU tests and integration with shared Python/Rust real-engine tests. Python is a comparator, not an oracle.

### 2. Scope

#### Architectural non-goals

The frontend will not own response/conversation storage, response-ID continuation or durable background execution. This is a lasting responsibility boundary. Transient request buffers and existing engine KV/prefix caches are unaffected. Full-history multi-turn requests remain supported, with roles, ordering and function-call associations preserved.

Responses will not introduce a second inference pipeline or forward generation through the Chat Completions HTTP endpoint or Python frontend. It uses the existing Rust serving and engine-client boundary. No engine wire-protocol, scheduler, kernel or tokenizer implementation change is proposed.

#### Initial delivery

Support foreground `POST /v1/responses`, buffered and streaming, with text, supported complete-history items, reasoning, client-executed function calls/results, supported generation controls, JSON structured output, existing image processing, usage, request context and disconnect cancellation. Reporting generation parameters resolved by shared Rust preparation is part of this contract.

The initial delivery excludes server-side tool execution/MCP/agent loops; Harmony-specific execution and serialized-history extensions; encrypted reasoning; a separate Responses render endpoint; audio/video or managed files; new model processors; output logprobs; `allowed_tools`; and automatic history truncation. These exclusions bound the first implementation without committing to later support. A request-local tool loop could be stateless: excluding orchestration is a separate responsibility decision, not a consequence of the storage rule.

Model qualification is separate from API scope. Reusing an existing processor

issues.title: [Bug]: Weight-loading/repacking memory is not reclaimed on discrete GPUs, forcing lower max-num-seqs / max-num-batched-tokens (Kimi K3, B200, fastsafetensors + DeepEP v2)
issues.body:
### Your current environment



- vLLM `v0.28.0`, `vllm/vllm-openai` container image
- 2–4 nodes x 8x NVIDIA **B200 SXM** (discrete GPU, 180 GB), GKE + LeaderWorkerSet
- Model: `moonshotai/Kimi-K3` (`mxfp4`), `--load-format fastsafetensors`, `--kv-cache-dtype fp8`
- Parallelism: TP4/TP8 + DP + `--enable-expert-parallel` (EP16 / EP32)
- All-to-all backends tested: **DeepEP v2** and NCCL (gIB RoCE)
- `NCCL_CUMEM_ENABLE=1`
- Also reproduced with speculative decoding (draft model `Inferact/Kimi-K3-DSpark`)



### 🐛 Describe the bug


On discrete GPUs, memory used during weight loading and `process_weights_after_loading` is retained inside PyTorch's caching allocator pool (`reserved - allocated`) rather than returned to the CUDA driver before the engine initializes communication buffers, profiles KV cache, or loads secondary models. In practice this causes startup OOM or forces significantly lower batch capacity.

**Observed behavior (reproducible):**

1. **2-node DeepEP v2 (`TP8_DP2_EP16`)** — with `--gpu-memory-utilization 0.88`, `--max-num-seqs 256 --max-num-batched-tokens 8192` OOMs during startup. Without a patch, we have to clamp parameters down to `--max-num-seqs 32 --max-num-batched-tokens 512 --gpu-memory-utilization 0.80`, which severely limits throughput.
2. **Speculative decoding (target `Kimi-K3` + draft `Kimi-K3-DSpark`, both via `fastsafetensors`)** — exhibits the same startup memory exhaustion pressure.
3. **With a 4-line memory cleanup patch injected into `process_weights_after_loading`, both workloads start cleanly and allow raising `--max-num-seqs` / `--max-num-batched-tokens` back up to `256 / 8192`:**

```python
def process_weights_after_loading(
    model: nn.Module, model_config: ModelConfig, target_device: torch.device
) -> None:
    import gc
    gc.collect()
    if torch.cuda.is_available():
        torch.cuda.empty_cache()
    ...
```

### Empirical VRAM Measurements (2x 8×B200 nodes, `TP8_DP2_EP16`, `v0.28.0`)

We instrumented `BaseModelLoader.load_model()` (`vllm/model_executor/model_loader/base_loader.py`) on 2x 8×B200 hosts (`178.351 GiB` total HBM per GPU) running `moonshotai/Kimi-K3` (`mxfp4`) + `Inferact/Kimi-K3-DSpark` with `--load-format fastsafetensors`:

| Model / Boundary | Arm A: Unpatched (`reserved_GiB` / `resv - alloc`) | Arm A: **`driver_free_GiB`** (`cudaMemGetInfo`) | Arm B: With `gc.collect() + empty_cache()` (`EMPTYCACHE_RETURNED`) | Arm B: **`driver_free_GiB`** (`cudaMemGetInfo`) |
| :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| **`Kimi-K3`: `05_before_load_weights`** | `129.352 GiB` (`0.286 GiB`) | `46.338 GiB` | `129.352 GiB` (`0.000 GiB`) | `46.338 GiB` |
| **`Kimi-K3`: `10_immediately_after_load_weights`** | `169.691 GiB` (**`40.626 GiB`**) | **`5.537 GiB`** | `129.352 GiB` (**`+40.342 GiB` freed**) | **`45.879 GiB`** |
| **`Kimi-K3`: `30_after_repack` (`mxfp4`)** | `174.734 GiB` (**`45.611 GiB`**) | **`0.494 GiB (494 MB!)`** | `129.365 GiB` (**`+5.141 GiB` freed**) | **`45.865 GiB`** |
| **`DSpark`: `10_immediately_after_load_weights`** | `141.395 GiB` (`10.335 GiB`) | `33.834 GiB` | `131.305 GiB` (**`+10.039 GiB` freed**) | **`43.925 GiB`** |

Key empirical findings on Rank 0 (`dev=0`):
- Immediately after `Kimi-K3` `load_weights()`, **`40.626 GiB`** of unallocated HBM is stranded in PyTorch's caching allocator pool (`reserved - allocated`), dropping CUDA driver free memory (`driver_free_GiB`) from `46.338 GiB` to **`5.537 GiB`**.

issues.title: [Bug]: On SM12x, fp8 block linear still selects DeepGEMM when E8M0 is disabled, which now hard-fails after the a6bbb80 pin
issues.body:
## Summary

`should_use_deepgemm_for_fp8_linear()` in `vllm/utils/deep_gemm.py` does not consider the scale format or the device family:

```python
return (
    supports_deep_gemm
    and output_dtype == torch.bfloat16
    and weight_shape[0] % N_MULTIPLE == 0
    and weight_shape[1] % K_MULTIPLE == 0
)
```

`DeepGemmLinearKernel.can_implement()` in `vllm/model_executor/kernels/linear/scaled_mm/deep_gemm.py` gates on exactly that, then stores `self.use_deep_gemm_e8m0 = is_deep_gemm_e8m0_used()` and forwards it to `fp8_gemm_nt`.

With the default `VLLM_USE_DEEP_GEMM_E8M0=1` this is fine on SM12x: the oracle returns `UE8M0` and the kernel is exact. But when E8M0 is disabled (the env var is documented and user settable), the oracle returns `FLOAT32` and vLLM still routes FP8 block linear to DeepGEMM, which has no working float32 scale path on SM12x.

## What happens on hardware

2x DGX Spark (GB10, sm_121), same nightly image (`0.29.1rc1.dev9+g2671fedfc`), only DeepGEMM differs. `fp8_gemm_nt`, block 128, bf16 out, reference `native_w8a8_block_matmul`, each case in a fresh process:

| M x N x K | float32 scales, DeepGEMM `ad1f1726` | float32 scales, DeepGEMM `a6bbb80` | ue8m0, both |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 x 128 x 256 | NaN in 0.78% of outputs | RuntimeError | rel 0.0 |
| 7 x 512 x 4096 | NaN in 22.1% | RuntimeError | rel 0.0 |
| 83 x 7168 x 4096 | NaN in 11.3% | RuntimeError | rel 9.05e-8 |
| 1 x 7168 x 4096 | NaN in 6.08% | RuntimeError | rel 0.0 |
| 4096 x 13824 x 16384 | NaN in 38.7% | RuntimeError | rel 6.57e-7 |

The error after the pin bump in #57218 is a host-side assert added by DeepGEMM#9:

```
RuntimeError: Assertion error (csrc/apis/sm120_dispatch.hpp:127):
sfa.scalar_type() == torch::kInt and sfb.scalar_type() == torch::kInt
```

So on SM12x with E8M0 disabled, main before #57218 produced silently wrong output, and main after #57218 raises at the first forward pass. The assert is the better of the two, but neither is what a user setting a documented env var should get.

Note that running `tests/kernels/quantization/test_block_fp8.py -k deep_gemm` on sm_121 against the older pin is not a safe reproducer: the first NaN case poisons the context and later cases fail with `CUDA error: unspecified launch failure`, and it can trigger Xid 43. Isolated single cases are clean.

## Suggested fix

Require the packed ue8m0 scale format on the 120 family when selecting the DeepGEMM FP8 linear kernel, for example by having `should_use_deepgemm_for_fp8_linear()` (or `DeepGemmLinearKernel.can_implement()`) return False when `DeepGemmQuantScaleFMT.from_oracle()` is `FLOAT32` and the device capability family is 120, so the existing non-DeepGEMM path is used instead.

## Scope of what I tested

Kernel level through vLLM's own wrappers (`vllm.utils.deep_gemm.fp8_gemm_nt`), weight-free, on sm_121. I did not run an end-to-end server with `VLLM_USE_DEEP_GEMM_E8M0=0`, and I have no sm_120 (RTX PRO 6000 class) board to confirm the same selection there, though the gate is family wide.

issues.title: [Bug]: Aria expert loading looks up w13_weight.weight / w2_weight.weight
issues.body:
### Your current environment

Reproduced on unmodified vLLM source commit `2c88fb131c7ae0be01907cd8c276911db5e7aad4`. The affected loader sources are unchanged in the subsequently checked main commit `64563d0ec4b761745d5babbc5750b263f0783926`.

```text
OS: Ubuntu 24.04.2 LTS, x86_64; kernel 6.17.0-1022-azure
CPU: AMD EPYC 7763 64-Core Processor (16 logical CPUs available)
Python: 3.12.3
PyTorch: 2.13.0+cpu; torch.version.cuda=None; CUDA available=False
Transformers: 5.17.0
vLLM Python source: 2c88fb131c7ae0be01907cd8c276911db5e7aad4
CPU native wheel commit: cd10ed6f9f6b37a8ace9cf380007e66fe12ec0c3
Execution: CPU, float32, no quantization, one Gloo rank, TP=1
MoE configuration: hidden_size=32, intermediate_size=64, 2 experts, top_k=1
```

The exact-source CPU wheel was unavailable during environment setup, so this run uses the native extensions from the [official CPU wheel for `cd10ed6f9`](https://wheels.vllm.ai/cd10ed6f9f6b37a8ace9cf380007e66fe12ec0c3/cpu/vllm/), a verified ancestor of the source revision. Python dependencies were reused read-only in an isolated uv-created environment; vLLM Python imports and Git blobs were verified against the clean source checkout. That checkout reports `vllm.__version__ == "dev"` because its generated `_version.py` is absent. The control below succeeds in the same environment. Current-source native binary parity and inference behavior remain untested.

### 🐛 Describe the bug

Aria expert checkpoint loading raises `AttributeError` before it can copy the tensors: `experts.fc1.weight` becomes `experts.gate_up_proj.weight`, then the fused expert loader tries to retrieve `w13_weight.weight`, although its actual parameter is named `w13_weight`. Independently loading `experts.fc2.weight` produces the corresponding `w2_weight.weight` error.

These are real checkpoint names. The reproducer gets its keys and tensors from Transformers' `AriaTextMoELayer.state_dict()` without renaming or transposing them. The [published `rhymes-ai/Aria` checkpoint index](https://huggingface.co/rhymes-ai/Aria/blob/53a09c77895d7025efa6239ea71cf1a8991064e8/model.safetensors.index.json) also contains `language_model.model.layers.0.mlp.experts.fc1.weight` and `language_model.model.layers.0.mlp.experts.fc2.weight` with the same expert suffixes.

Expected: both authentic expert checkpoint names resolve to the routed expert parameters and proceed to tensor loading. Actual: the loader raises the parameter-name exceptions below. This blocks the reproduced Aria weight-loading path before inference.

#### Minimal CPU reproduction

In a CPU vLLM environment with the packages above, save this as `repro_aria_expert.py`. It constructs the real vLLM Aria MoE layer and uses the stock `AriaTextModel` mapper, `AutoWeightsLoader`, `MoERunner`, and `RoutedExperts`. There are no mocked loaders, manually registered expert parameters, downloaded model weights, or checkpoint-name adaptations.

```python
"""Reproduce Aria expert checkpoint-name loading on an installed CPU vLLM."""

import sys
import tempfile
from pathlib import Path

import torch
from transformers import AriaTextConfig
from transformers.models.aria.modeling_aria import AriaTextMoELayer as HFMoE

from vllm.config import VllmConfig, set_current_vllm_config
from vllm.distributed import (
    cleanup_dist_env_and_memory,
    init_distributed_environment,
    initialize_model_parallel,
)
from vllm.model_executor.models.aria import AriaTextModel, AriaTextMoELayer
from vllm.model_executor.models

issues.title: [Bug]: DFlash2 (dflash method) deterministic cumulative OOB — engine dies with CUDA IMA / Xid 31 after ~11k decode steps under sampling load (sm_80, v0.27.1)
issues.body:
### Your current environment

- vLLM 0.27.1 (vanilla PyPI wheel, `pip install vllm==0.27.1`), also exercised with the community patch set from syv-ai/qwen38-27b-rtx3090 (verify.sh all-pass; the split-KV spec-decode attention envs — `VLLM_SPEC_DECODE_ATTN`/`_QMAX`, `VLLM_DFLASH2_*` — are upstream in 0.27.1)
- GPU: NVIDIA CMP 170HX — GA100 silicon, **sm_80**, 64 GiB HBM2e (compute-equivalent A100-class SKU), headless
- Driver 610.43.02, CUDA UMD 13.3, Ubuntu 24.04
- torch 2.13.0, flashinfer-python 0.6.16.post3, flashinfer-cubin 0.6.13
- Target: Qwen3.8-27B W4A16 AutoRound (compressed-tensors); Draft: `syvai/Qwen3.8-27B-DFlash2-W4A16`

### 🐛 Describe the bug

DFlash2 speculative decoding (`--speculative-config {"method":"dflash", ...}`) accumulates an out-of-bounds condition in the decode loop and kills the engine with a CUDA illegal-memory-access after a **fixed cumulative number of decode steps (~11k with k=7)**, regardless of scheduling or CUDA-graph configuration. `dmesg` shows `Xid 31, MMU Fault ... FAULT_PDE ACCESS_TYPE_VIRT_READ`. Greedy (`temperature 0`) load does not crash; sampling load crashes deterministically at the same cumulative point.

**Repro** (server config: `--attention-backend FLASH_ATTN --kv-cache-dtype bfloat16 --max-model-len 262144 --max-num-seqs 1`, env `VLLM_SPEC_DECODE_ATTN=1 VLLM_SPEC_DECODE_ATTN_QMAX=8 VLLM_DFLASH2_LOOKUP=1`):

```bash
# repeat rounds back-to-back against the same live server:
vllm bench serve --backend openai-chat --base-url http://127.0.0.1:8000 \
  --endpoint /v1/chat/completions --model <served-name> --tokenizer <target-hf> \
  --dataset-name random --input-len 8192 --output-len 512 \
  --num-prompts 12 --max-concurrency 4 --temperature 1 --ignore-eos
```

Round 1: 12/12 pass. Round 2: engine dies (requests 11–12 of round 2 every time).

**Bisect matrix** — crashes at the same cumulative decode-step count in **all** of:

| variable | values tried |
|---|---|
| async scheduling | on / off |
| `VLLM_DFLASH2_LOOKUP` | 1 / 0 |
| `VLLM_DFLASH2_TORCH_TOPK` | 1 |
| CUDA graphs | full / piecewise / `--enforce-eager` (eager surfaces the error at the next sync op, kernel unnamed) |
| `--max-num-seqs` | 1 / 2 / 8 (pure C1 geometry via queueing still crashes) |
| `num_speculative_tokens` | 7 → crash ≈11k steps; 3 → delayed to ≈15k steps, same failure |

`VLLM_SPEC_DECODE_ATTN=0` is the only non-crashing setting, but there acceptance length collapses to ~1.1 (the non-split-KV verify fallback does not verify multi-query blocks correctly), so speculation is effectively off and it is not a valid control.

### Hints

- Related community report: syv-ai/qwen38-27b-rtx3090#34 (Xid-31 family, flashinfer+MTP path, recurring at a fixed fault address) and our fuller field report syv-ai/qwen38-27b-rtx3090#72.
- The accumulating-step-count signature points at per-step bookkeeping in the V2 spec-decode path (draft/verify ring buffers or the split-KV verify partial buffers that are "sized once" by design) rather than a scheduler race.
- Happy to run targeted debug builds (e.g. compute-sanitizer memcheck on the repro, or a branch with bounds checks in the verify path) on this card — it reproduces within ~6 minutes of sustained load.

### Before submitting:

- [x] Search similar questions: I searched for "dflash illegal memory access", "Xid 31 speculative", "DFlash2 OOB"; closest matches are community issues above; no upstream report found for the dflash V2 path.

issues.title: [Feature]: [CPU][GLM5Next][KDA] Add CPU KDA backend for GLM-5.3-Flash
issues.body:
### 🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch

## Motivation

GLM-5.3-Flash (`Glm5NextForConditionalGeneration`) is a hybrid model containing both:

* sparse MLA layers
* KDA (Kimi Delta Attention / gated delta-rule) linear-attention layers

Even if GLM5Next's sparse MLA / KeyPool path is made CPU-compatible, the model still cannot execute end-to-end on CPU without a KDA backend.

I would like to request native CPU support for GLM5Next KDA.

## Current state

The GLM5Next KDA implementation currently lives under the accelerator-specific path:

```text
vllm/models/glm5next/nvidia/kda.py
```

and uses GPU-oriented Flash Linear Attention / Triton operators such as:

```text
chunk_kda_with_fused_gate
fused_recurrent_kda
```

There does not appear to be a corresponding:

```text
vllm/models/glm5next/cpu/kda.py
```

or other CPU KDA execution path for GLM5Next on current `main`.

This makes KDA an independent CPU blocker from sparse MLA / KeyPool support.

GLM-5.3-Flash has a large number of KDA layers, so this cannot reasonably be worked around by supporting only the sparse-MLA portion of the model.

## Related CPU infrastructure already exists

The CPU backend already has substantial support for related linear-attention/state-space workloads.

In particular, current CPU platform code contains an accelerated GDN path using:

```text
AMX tiles
or
AVX-512 BF16 / VDPBF16PS
```

and vLLM already has CPU machinery for stateful hybrid models, including:

* recurrent state caches
* convolution state
* chunked prefill
* decode
* hybrid KV/state-cache management

KDA is not identical to GDN, but they are closely related enough that it may be possible to reuse much of this infrastructure.

## KDA-specific work

As I understand it, GLM5Next KDA needs CPU equivalents for the KDA-specific operations around the existing gated-delta/state machinery, including:

```text
Q/K/V short convolution
        │
        ▼
KDA gate computation
        │
        ▼
chunked gated-delta prefill
        │
        ▼
final recurrent state
        │
        ▼
single-token recurrent decode
        │
        ▼
gated/RMSNorm output
```

The important parts include:

* q/k/v convolution and convolution-state update
* KDA gate calculation
* per-channel decay/gating behavior
* `chunk_kda_with_fused_gate` equivalent for prefill
* `fused_recurrent_kda` equivalent for decode
* initial-state gathering
* final-state writeback
* mixed decode/prefill handling
* state-cache addressing
* chunk boundaries
* prefix-cache/state restore correctness

## Requested feature

Add a CPU KDA backend for GLM5Next.

A correctness-first implementation would be useful even before full AMX optimization.

One possible structure could be:

```text
vllm/models/glm5next/
├── common/
├── nvidia/
├── amd/
└── cpu/
    └── kda.py
```

with explicit platform dispatch rather than allowing CPU to reach the NVIDIA implementation.

## Possible implementation phases

### Phase 1: reference CPU implementation

Provide a functional PyTorch/C++ CPU implementation for:

* short convolution
* chunked KDA prefill
* recurrent KDA decode
* KDA gate/output
* state gather/scatter

The initial goal would be correctness and end-to-end execution.

### Phase 2: reuse existing CPU GDN kernels

Where the mathematical operations overlap with the existing CPU GDN backend, share or extend those implementations rather than creating duplicate infrastructure.

### Phase 3: x86 optimization

Optimize the expensive GEMM/state operations with:

* A

issues.title: DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash fails to start on 4x H20 (587GiB RAM): MEMCG OOM from host shmem (TP weight shards), not GPU
issues.body:
**DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash fails to start on 4x H20 (limited node RAM): MEMCG OOM driven by host shmem (TP weight shards), not GPU capacity**

## Environment
- Model: `deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash` (~510GB on disk; Engram memory ~189 GiB)
- Hardware: **4x H20** (96 GB HBM each = 384 GB total GPU), **node RAM only ~587 GiB**
- vLLM: nightly `v0.29.1rc1.dev128+gcd10ed6f9` (has `DeepseekV41ForCausalLM`, `deepseek_v41` registered)

## Problem
Worker processes are killed by **MEMCG OOM** during model loading, driven almost entirely by **host shared memory (shmem)**, not anonymous memory:

```
Memory cgroup out of memory: Killed process (VLLM::Worker_TP)
  total-vm: 824088588 kB, anon-rss: 3131928 kB, file-rss: 74760 kB, shmem-rss: 150143716 kB
  constraint: CONSTRAINT_MEMCG
```

Each of the 4 TP workers reports **shmem-rss ~143 GB** (anon-rss only ~3 GB). The kernel OOM-killer clears all 4 `VLLM::Worker_TP` processes one by one. `/dev/shm` is empty (`df -h /dev/shm` shows 200G, 52K used), and `/proc/meminfo Shmem` is only ~96 GB, so this shmem is **not /dev/shm** — it is the shared memory used for the TP-distributed weight tensors (memfd / shared anonymous tensors). 4 × 143 GB ≈ 573 GB shmem + Engram ≈ exceeds the node's ~587 GiB physical RAM.

## What we already tried (none fix the shmem wall)
- `--cpu-offload-gb` 200 → 50: no change in death point → rules out host offload as the driver
- `--safetensors-load-strategy lazy`: **fixed** the earlier page-cache OOM (both Engram offloads now pass), but the shmem death remains
- `--no-cudagraph`: extended survival (~51s → ~87s) but the worker still dies the same way
- `--max-num-seqs` 8: no effect (death happens before KV allocation, during weight/shmem load)

## Question
For a node with **limited host RAM** (~587 GiB) but adequate GPU (4x H20 = 384 GB), is there a way to keep the TP weight shards **resident on GPU instead of host shared memory**, or otherwise reduce the ~143 GB shmem per worker so V4.1-Flash can start? Or is 4x H20 / this RAM budget simply not viable for V4.1-Flash?

Community guidance suggests 4x H20 is "below the comfortable threshold" and Engram KV offload / heavier quantization are options — but those reduce GPU usage, not the host shmem that is our binding constraint. Any pointer on the shmem allocation mechanism (where the ~143 GB per worker comes from and whether it can be moved to GPU) would help.

issues.title: [Bug] CUDA graph memory estimate under-reserves → OOM during graph capture at high `--gpu-memory-utilization`
issues.body:
## Summary
With `--kv-cache-dtype nvfp4` and `--gpu-memory-utilization 0.98`, the engine passes the
KV-cache allocation check but then crashes during CUDA-graph capture with
`torch.OutOfMemoryError`. Dropping to `0.97` boots and serves fine. The KV pool is sized
using `cudagraph_memory_estimate` from `profile_cudagraph_memory()`, but that estimate does
not leave enough headroom for the *real* capture once the (larger) KV pool is allocated.

## Environment
- vLLM: `0.29.1rc1.dev339+gda9888462` (commit `da9888462`)
- GPU: NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5090 Laptop GPU (24 GB, SM12x), driver 610.57.04
- torch `2.13.0+cu130`, CUDA 13.0
- Model: Qwen3.8-27B NVFP4 (hybrid attention / linear-attention)
- `VLLM_ATTENTION_BACKEND=FLASHINFER`

## Reproduction
```bash
VLLM_ATTENTION_BACKEND=FLASHINFER vllm serve <model> \
  --kv-cache-dtype nvfp4 \
  --gpu-memory-utilization 0.98 \
  --max-model-len 124000 \
  --max-num-seqs 1 \
  --max-num-batched-tokens 2048 \
  --enable-prefix-caching \
  --trust-remote-code --dtype bfloat16
```

## Observed
At `0.98` (crashes):
```
INFO  [gpu_worker.py:642]  Available KV cache memory: 2.97 GiB
INFO  [kv_cache_utils.py]  GPU KV cache size: 150,745 tokens, Maximum concurrency for 124,000 tokens
INFO  [model_runner.py]    Graph capturing finished in 1 secs, took 0.46 GiB   # profiling estimate
DEBUG [gpu_worker.py:641]  ... Total non KV cache memory: 19.57 GiB ...
ERROR [engine/core.py:1378] torch.OutOfMemoryError: CUDA out of memory.
      Tried to allocate 136.00 MiB. GPU 0 has a total capacity of 23.46 GiB
      of which 120.88 MiB is free ...
```
At `0.97` (works):
```
INFO  [gpu_worker.py:642]  Available KV cache memory: 2.73 GiB
INFO  [kv_cache_utils.py]  GPU KV cache size: 138,588 tokens
INFO  [gpu_worker.py:828]  CUDA graph pool memory: 0.04 GiB (actual), 0.46 GiB (estimated)
```

## Analysis
`determine_available_memory()` (`vllm/v1/worker/gpu_worker.py`) sizes the pool as:
```
available_kv = requested_memory - non_kv_cache_memory - cudagraph_memory_estimate
```
with `cudagraph_memory_estimate = model_runner.profile_cudagraph_memory()`.

`profile_cudagraph_memory()` (`vllm/v1/worker/gpu_model_runner.py`) captures a small sample
of graphs (`descs[:2]` per mode) into a temporary pool, measures the delta, and extrapolates
with `first_capture + (N-1) * per_graph`. For this model it reports **0.46 GiB**.

The problem: the *real* capture (`capture_model()`) runs **after** the full KV pool is
allocated, in a tighter memory environment. At 0.98 the pool is larger (150,745 tok / 2.97 GiB
vs 138,588 / 2.73 GiB at 0.97) and the real capture OOMs with only 120.88 MiB free — i.e. the
0.46 GiB reservation did not leave enough headroom for the actual capture. (The `0.04 GiB
(actual)` figure is the net delta of the real capture, not the total graph footprint, because
most graph memory is already resident from the profiling pass.)

## Suggested fixes (any of)
1. Apply a safety margin to the estimate (e.g. reserve ~1.5× the measured graph memory).
2. Profile the graph capture **with the KV pool allocated** so the estimate reflects the real
   memory layout.
3. Measure the real capture footprint and reserve a conservative upper bound.

## Workaround
- `--gpu-memory-utilization 0.97` (boots and serves; ~138K NVFP4 KV tokens), or
- `--enforce-eager` at 0.98 (no graph memory, ~166K KV tokens, slower decode).

## Notes
- This is specific to running close to the memory ceiling with CUDA graphs enabled; the
  binding constraint is graph memo

issues.title: [RFC]: Bound frontend drain latency for bulk aborts and long non-streaming completions
issues.body:
# Motivation.

Bulk abort is expected to be the fast path for pausing online RL generation,
but its latency can scale with all output retained by the frontend. In a
DP8/EP8/TP1 deployment with eight API server processes, aborting 2,000
non-streaming completion requests at a reported approximately 3,500 generated
tokens per request produced 96-177 seconds of frontend tail latency. Actual
returned means were 4,850-5,445 tokens because generation continued while the
frontend lagged. The engines had already accepted the abort; API processes
were still draining queued outputs,
detokenizing sampled logprobs, constructing response models, materializing
Python dictionaries, and encoding JSON.

The largest amplifier was API-process load imbalance. The parent enabled
`SO_REUSEPORT`, but all workers inherited copies of one socket and therefore
shared one accept queue. In one run, the busiest API process owned 1,492 of
2,000 requests. Balanced DP-engine load did not imply balanced frontend load.

This matters beyond RL pause. The same work appears when long non-streaming
completion requests finish or are aborted together, especially when sampled
logprobs or token IDs are returned. A fast model can produce outputs faster
than one Python frontend process can consume and serialize them.

This RFC follows the completed pause/resume API RFC #32103, whose follow-up
list explicitly called out better abort handling. It does not change pause
mode semantics or DPEP coordination. Searches of all issues and open PRs using
pause/abort, frontend serialization, logprobs, API server, and reuseport terms
found no overlapping proposal or implementation. Related work is
complementary:

- #56754 drains in-process requests before sleep.
- #52875 reduces per-frame cost for simple streaming completions.
- #47933 preserves `finish_reason="abort"` for scale-out token streams.

## Reproduction and evidence

The primary setup used two GB200 nodes, DP8/EP8/TP1, eight API servers, 2,000
requests, and sampled `logprobs=0`. A four-layer checkpoint made the frontend
bottleneck easy to reproduce; the final candidate was also validated with the
full 78-layer MXFP8 checkpoint.

On the reduced model, the unmodified frontend took 96.18 and 177.12 seconds
from pause to its last response serialization in two runs. The measured
seven-file candidate took 3.38 seconds at 7.28 million returned tokens, and
5.18 seconds at 10.08 million returned tokens versus 96.18 seconds at 10.89
million unmodified. The six-file patch proposed here differs only by removal
of a null-result lazy-context change and was itself measured as the valid
2.924-second `no_lazy_context` leave-one-out arm.

On the full model, one unmodified baseline was 6.97 seconds frontend and 7.44
seconds through all client results, with a balanced 187-270 requests per
frontend. Four additional unmodified runs using a two-process client that
concentrated connections on fewer workers reached 8.92-21.10-second frontend
tails, with 462-907 requests on the busiest process. Two used the 3,500-token
trigger and two used 3,800. They have no patched counterpart and are baseline
evidence, not an A/B comparison.

Two seven-file-candidate repeats completed frontend serialization in 3.63 and
3.90 seconds and all client parsing in 3.81 and 4.19 seconds; waiting for both
the pause HTTP response and all client results took 3.81 and 7.67 seconds. This
validates parity and absence of regression at full scale. It does not reproduce
the reduced model's

issues.title: [Bug] Hybrid mamba align precopy: illegal memory access on prefix-cache resume with explicit --block-size (state column seeded with wrong block size)
issues.body:
### Your current environment

vLLM 0.27.1, V2 GPU runner, single RTX 3090 (SM86), CUDA 12.x, WSL2 Ubuntu 24.04 (also reproduces the same way on bare metal by code inspection). Model: Qwen3.8-27B (hybrid GDN/mamba + full attention), W4A16.

### 🐛 Describe the bug

`MambaHybridModelState.add_request` (v1/worker/gpu/model_states/mamba_hybrid.py) seeds the running mamba state column with the **CLI/attention block size** instead of the **mamba KV-cache group's block size**:

```python
self._mamba_state_idx_gpu[req_index].fill_(
    (new_req_data.num_computed_tokens - 1) // self.cache_config.block_size
)
```

On hybrid models the mamba group's `block_size` is derived from page matching (e.g. 2176 for a Qwen3-Next-style hybrid) and generally differs from `cache_config.block_size` whenever the user passes `--block-size` explicitly (required e.g. for quantized-KV setups whose tile size dictates the block, in our case 128).

With `--block-size 128 --enable-prefix-caching --mamba-cache-mode align`, the **second** request over a cached prefix crashes: a resume with `num_computed_tokens=100096` seeds `state_idx = (100096-1)//128 = 781` instead of `(100096-1)//2176 = 45`. The fused align precopy (`precopy_mamba_align_fused_kernel`) then reads `block_table[req, 781]` in a table with only ~61 columns, gets a garbage block id, and dies with:

```
RuntimeError: Triton Error [CUDA]: an illegal memory access was encountered
  File "vllm/v1/worker/gpu/model_states/mamba_hybrid.py", line 201, in preprocess_state
  File "vllm/v1/worker/mamba_utils.py", line 826, in run_fused_precopy
```

(confirmed as the faulting kernel with `CUDA_LAUNCH_BLOCKING=1`).

First requests are unaffected (`num_computed == 0` seeds `-1` regardless of divisor), so in practice this looks like a spurious crash that only appears on the second request over a >1-block cached prefix — easy to misattribute.

**Repro:** any hybrid (mamba+attention) model with `--block-size <n>` where n != the mamba group block size, `--enable-prefix-caching`, `--mamba-cache-mode align`; send the same multi-block prompt twice.

### Fix (verified)

Seed with the mamba spec's block size. `_mamba_spec` is populated lazily by the first batch's `preprocess_state`; a resume can only happen after some batch has run, and fresh requests seed `-1` either way, so the fallback is safe:

```python
mamba_bs = (self._mamba_spec.block_size
            if self._mamba_spec is not None
            else self.cache_config.block_size)
self._mamba_state_idx_gpu[req_index].fill_(
    (new_req_data.num_computed_tokens - 1) // mamba_bs
)
```

Verified on the setup above: two-turn 102k-token needle test, turn 2 resumes from 100,096 cached tokens, both answers correct, turn-2 latency 6.3 s vs ~190 s cold. Happy to turn this into a PR if wanted.

### Before submitting a new issue...

- [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

issues.title: [Feature]: Fast Start For vLLM
issues.body:
## Overview

Fast Start reduces vLLM startup time by avoiding repeated checkpoint loading, weight processing, and kernel autotuning during engine restarts and scaling events.

The core design uses a persistent per-GPU weight daemon. The daemon loads and processes model weights once, keeps sharded weights in GPU memory, and exposes them to new vLLM engines through CUDA IPC or a multi-node transport.

When a compatible cache is unavailable, vLLM falls back to the existing checkpoint loader.

## Design Goals

- Reuse processed GPU weights across engine instances.
- Support TP, PP, EP, multi-node deployments, and MTP.
- Support quantized formats including FP8 and FP4.
- Cache autotune results with hardware- and version-aware keys.
- Preserve correctness through strict cache validation.
- Provide a reliable fallback path for cache misses and failures.

## Cache Validation

Cache entries are identified using model and checkpoint identity, quantization configuration, parallelism settings, GPU architecture, vLLM protocol version, and other relevant runtime metadata.

Incompatible entries must never be silently reused. Cache misses, stale daemon connections, and validation failures produce diagnostics and fall back to the normal loading path when enabled.

- Cached and regular loading produce equivalent model outputs.
- Cache failures do not compromise correctness or availability.
- Startup, cache-hit, fallback, transfer, and autotune timings are observable.

issues.title: [Bug][Reasoning] kimi_k3: non-streaming path classifies truncated reasoning as content (inconsistent with streaming path)
issues.body:
### Report

The `kimi_k3` reasoning parser's non-streaming fallback misclassifies truncated reasoning output as `content`, leaving `reasoning_content` as `null`. The streaming path classifies the exact same output as reasoning, so the two paths disagree.

### Root cause

`KimiK3ReasoningParser.extract_reasoning` in `vllm/reasoning/kimi_k3_reasoning_parser.py` (main @ f94666b60d):

```python
m_open = self._think_open_re.search(model_output)
content_start = m_open.end() if m_open is not None else 0
# if there is no think channel at all, everything is content
if m_open is None and self._think_close_re.search(model_output) is None:
    return None, self._content_after_reasoning(model_output, request)
```

The key fact is on the template side: when thinking is enabled, the Kimi K3 chat template ends the prompt with the think **open** marker (`<|open|>think<|sep|>`) as a generation prefix — the model never generates the open marker itself. So in generated text:

- the open marker is (almost) always absent;
- the close marker (`<|close|>think<|sep|>`) is absent whenever the output is truncated (e.g. `max_tokens` smaller than the reasoning length) or generation stops early.

That combination falls into the branch above and the whole reasoning text is returned as `content` with `reasoning=None`.

Meanwhile, the streaming path in the same file (`extract_reasoning_streaming`) treats any text with no close marker as reasoning:

```python
# no close marker anywhere -> still reasoning
return DeltaMessage(reasoning=reasoning_delta)
```

So for identical truncated output: `stream=true` returns it as `reasoning_content`, `stream=false` returns it as `content`. This also diverges from the upstream basic parsers (`vllm/reasoning/basic_parsers.py`), where a missing end token means the whole output stays reasoning (`return model_output, None`).

### Repro

Serve Kimi K3 with `--reasoning-parser kimi_k3`, then:

```bash
curl http://<server>/v1/chat/completions -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{
  "model": "auto",
  "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "reason step by step: 3 apples cost 12 yuan, how much for 7?"}],
  "max_tokens": 10,
  "stream": false
}' | jq '.choices[0].message'
```

Returns:

```json
{
  "content": "The user asks to reason step by step about a math problem. I only need ",
  "reasoning_content": null
}
```

With `"stream": true`, the same generation arrives as `reasoning_content` deltas instead.

### Suggested fix

When thinking is enabled and neither think marker appears in the output, treat the whole output as unterminated reasoning instead of content:

```python
if m_open is None and self._think_close_re.search(model_output) is None:
    return (model_output or None, None)
```

Rationale: with thinking enabled the template always opens the think channel as a generation prefix, so the case the current comment targets ("no think channel at all") cannot actually occur in generated output — truncated reasoning is the realistic scenario behind "no markers". This also aligns the non-streaming fallback with the streaming path and with the upstream basic parsers. The `thinking=false` branch is unaffected.

Note the same fallback exists since the parser was introduced in #50093 and was preserved by the refactor in #50886; vllm-ascend vendors this file verbatim, so downstream is affected identically. Happy to submit a PR with the fix plus regression tests (no existing test locks the current fallback behavior — `tests/reasoning/test_ki

issues.title: [RFC]: Share KV transfer planning primitives across KV connectors
issues.body:
### 🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch

#### Problem

Cross-engine KV transfer (PD disaggregation) must, per cache group, classify the KV cache spec type (attention / SSM / other) and compute how local TP shards map onto a remote engine's TP shards — slice by TP ratio, replicate, or copy whole. When this is wrong it usually fails silently: mismatched slicing corrupts state (e.g. conv-state bytes landing in the wrong sub-projection).

The only in-tree implementation of this planning logic lives inside the NIXL connector (`nixl/tp_mapping.py`, underscore-private helpers). The cost is observable today:

- The same subtle bugs get fixed twice. Mamba prefill truncation ordering was fixed independently in #53523 (NIXL) and #53663 (Mooncake) within the same week.
- New model architectures need connector-specific fixes on the Mooncake side (#52516, #53078, #55523), while NIXL absorbs the same class of change through generic machinery (#53780).
- Reuse is already happening piecemeal: #53078 reuses `derive_mamba_conv_split` from `v1/ssm_conv_transfer_utils.py`, a framework extraction from NIXL.

#### Proposal

Make this planning logic a shared connector-framework module with a public, connector-agnostic API, and migrate connectors onto it in stages:

1. **Substrate** (draft: #57309). `v1/transfer_planning.py` hosts spec-type classification (`is_attention_spec`, `is_ssm_spec`, `get_representative_spec_type`) and local-to-remote TP mapping (`TPMapping`, `compute_tp_mapping`). NIXL consumes it unchanged; MooncakeConnector adopts the classification helpers; contract tests pin the classification vocabulary. NIXL-specific structs (e.g. `ReadSpec`) stay NIXL-local.
2. **Region descriptions.** Extract the per-region transfer-description construction from `nixl/base_worker.py` registration into the same module, so a connector declares region facts (type, layout, shard rule) and the shared code computes the plan. NIXL behavior unchanged.
3. **MooncakeConnector adoption.** Replace the private region planning (`_get_transfer_regions` and related) with the shared planner after #53078 / #55523 land and provide the behavioral baseline. Wire format unchanged.

Invariants across all stages: NIXL behavior unchanged, wire formats unchanged, and connector-specific concerns (transports, the Mooncake Store canonical layout) stay connector-local.

### Alternatives

- **Status quo (two implementations)**: correctness fixes must be applied twice (#53523 / #53663) and the copies drift over time.
- **Mooncake imports from the `nixl` package**: a layering violation — it couples one connector to another connector's private internals, so every NIXL change risks breaking it.
- **Single big-bang migration**: harder to review and bisect; the substrate stage is independently useful to any connector.

### Additional context

- Stage 1 is open as draft PR #57309, including the duplicate-work check against open PRs.
- I am willing to implement and maintain the follow-up stages. Feedback from NIXL and Mooncake connector maintainers on the stage-2/3 boundary would be appreciated.

issues.title: [Feature]: Support multi-turn conversation for OpenAI Response API
issues.body:
### 🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch

I wanted to test **GPT-OSS-120B** served via **vLLM** using AI coding agents such as **opencode** and **codex**.
For these agents, **tool calling and multi-turn conversations are essential**, and according to OpenAI's documentation, the **`/v1/responses` endpoint** is the recommended API for this use case.

#### Observed behavior

When configuring both agents (opencode and codex) to call the model through the **`/v1/responses` endpoint**, everything works smoothly for the **first request**:
vLLM responds correctly and returns a valid output.

However, when continuing the conversation (**multi-turn interaction**), at the very second request, vLLM fails and returns **validation errors**.

The failure seems to occur because these agents send the conversation history using the **OpenAI Responses API format**, which vLLM does **not currently support**.

vLLM expects inputs formatted according to the **Chat Completions API**:

```json
{
  "messages": [
    {"role": "user", "content": "Hello"},
    {"role": "assistant", "content": "Hi there!"},
    {"role": "user", "content": "How are you?"}
  ]
}
```

The agents send requests using the **Responses API format**:

```json
{
  "input": [
    {
      "type": "message",
      "role": "user",
      "content": [{ "type": "input_text", "text": "Hello" }]
    },
    {
      "type": "message",
      "role": "assistant",
      "content": [{ "type": "output_text", "text": "Hi there!" }]
    },
    {
      "type": "reasoning",
      "encrypted_content": null,
      "summary": []
    },
    {
      "type": "message",
      "role": "user",
      "content": [{ "type": "input_text", "text": "How are you?" }]
    }
  ]
}
```

Error returned by vLLM:

```
400 Bad Request: 356 validation errors
- Input should be a valid string
- Field required: ResponseReasoningItem.id
- Field required: ResponseOutputMessage.id
- ...
```


#### Question / Feature request

Are there plans to support the **OpenAI Responses API** in vLLM?
This would enable proper **multi-turn conversations and tool-calling workflows** for AI agents such as **opencode**, **codex**, and potentially others that rely on this API.


### Steps to reproduce

| Agent    | Version | Command                                                                                                    | Result                                   |
| -------- | ------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------- |
| opencode | v1.1.31 | `opencode run "Hello, this is my first test message."`                                                     | ✅ Success — `"Hello! Nice to meet you."` |
| opencode | v1.1.31 | `opencode run --continue "This is my second message. What was my first message about?"`                    | ❌ 348 validation errors                  |
| codex    | v0.88.0 | `VLLM_API_KEY=test codex exec "Hello, this is my first test message."`                                     | ✅ Success — `"Hello! 👋"`                |
| codex    | v0.88.0 | `VLLM_API_KEY=test codex exec resume --last "This is my second message. What was my first message about?"` | ❌ 356 validation errors                  |


I attached:

* The command used to launch the vLLM server:
```
docker run -d \
  --name vllm \
  --restart unless-stopped \
  --runtime nvidia \
  -e NVIDIA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=all \
  -p 8000:8000 \
  -v huggingface-cache:/root/.cach

issues.title: [RFC]: Support VLLM Container Snapshot with Checkpoint/Restore in Userspace (CRIU)
issues.body:
## Background and Motivation

LLM serving has a long cold-start path: vLLM loads model weights,
allocates device memory, initializes distributed communication, starts
EngineCore/API-server transports, and may compile or capture execution state.
Container checkpoint/restore can reduce recovery and scale-up latency by
restoring an already initialized container site rather than repeating that work.

However, vLLM allocates device resources which are out range of host side, and container local IP will be changed when restore. Therefore, there needs a pair of explicit lifecycle APIs:

1. suspend API: Before checkpoint, vLLM notifies Worker processes to back up their allocated
   device resources and device state to host storage (device-to-host, D2H).
2. resume API: After restore, vLLM clears stale runtime state, rebuilds its ZMQ connections
   and Scheduler state, and notifies Worker processes to restore their device resources and device state.

Container restore does not make all vLLM runtime resources usable. The restored
container can receive a new network address, so TCP-based ZMQ connections must
be recreated. Device resources also need recovery before inference resumes. An
external checkpoint controller cannot perform these operations inside vLLM, so
vLLM coordinates them and the device plugin restores Worker state.

## Scope and Assumptions

This RFC covers restoring an initialized vLLM V1 serving process. The external
controller is responsible for triggering the container checkpoint/restore and
for ensuring that no request is executing in the worker forward path at the
checkpoint boundary. This RFC does not define the container runtime's snapshot
format or scheduling policy.

The lifecycle is opt-in. A deployment without `--snapshot-config` retains the
normal cold-start and serving paths unchanged.

## Proposed Change

Introduce an opt-in container snapshot lifecycle for vLLM V1.

### Configuration

Add `--snapshot-config` with an optional `snapshot_metadata` path. The path
points to a JSON object mounted in the container; metadata fields consumed by
vLLM must contain string values. It supplies deployment information that is
only known after restore, such as the current data-parallel master address.

Snapshot APIs and restore-specific behavior are enabled only when
`--snapshot-config` is supplied. When an API client manages remote
data-parallel EngineCore processes, lifecycle calls require `snapshot_metadata`
so those processes can reconnect to the restored container address.

### Lifecycle APIs

vLLM propagates each API through the existing API server -> EngineCoreClient ->
EngineCore -> ModelExecutor -> Worker path:

1. `POST /suspend` prepares vLLM for checkpoint and invokes Worker `suspend`.
   A successful response permits the external controller to create the
   checkpoint.
2. `POST /device_unlock` invokes Worker `device_unlock` in the original
   container after checkpoint creation.
3. `POST /resume` reconnects the EngineCore control path, invokes Worker
   `resume`, and refreshes the Scheduler state required for serving. A
   successful response permits inference to resume.

A process-shared lifecycle monitor serializes each operation, prevents duplicate
execution when multiple API server processes receive the same request, records
successful completion, and clears an in-progress gate after a failed attempt so
the operation can be retried.

### Responsibilities

Core vLLM preserves EngineCore transport identities, recreates T

### 🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch

DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash landed with #56214 / #56228, and the tracking issue #56400
lists it as verified on **H200, GB200, GB300, MI350X**. There is no Ampere
(sm_80) path, and — unlike sm_120, which has field reports in #56700, #56837 and
#56892 — nobody appears to be working on one: searching issues and PRs for
`V4.1` combined with `ampere` / `A100` / `sm80` / `A800` returns only #50576,
which is the **V4** (not 4.1) Ampere tracking issue I opened in July.

This issue tracks getting `DeepseekV41ForCausalLM` running on 8×A100/A800
(sm_80), and offers to do the work. I previously ported DeepSeek-V4-Flash and
V4-Flash-0731 (DSpark) to this same box and reported the result in #50576.

A800 is still the most widely deployed 80 GB datacenter GPU in China, and
V4.1-Flash's 510 GB of weights fit on a single 8×80 GB node, so there is real
demand for this.

### Environment

| reference kernel | sm_80 | detail |
|---|---|---|
| `sparse_attn` (BF16 gather + online softmax + attn sink) | **works** | compiles and matches a torch reference, max rel err 2.9e-3 (bf16-level) at h=64, d=512, topk=512 |
| `act_quant` (bf16 → fp8 e4m3 + fp32 scales) | **works** | conversion only, no MMA |
| `fp4_act_quant` (bf16 → fp4 + e8m0 scales) | **works** | conversion only, no MMA |
| `fp8_gemm` | **fails** | TileLang lowers `T.gemm` on fp8 operands to CUTLASS `SM89_16x8x32_F32E4M3E4M3F32_TN`; device assert `CUTE_ARCH_MMA_F32_SM89_ENABLED` |
| `fp4_gemm` | **fails** | same wall |

The useful conclusion: the *sparse-MLA attention math itself is portable to
Ampere* — what is not portable is narrow-precision **MMA**, because sm_80 has no
FP8/FP4 tensor-core instruction. That is a much smaller problem than it looks,
since vLLM already routes narrow-precision GEMM on older arches through Marlin
and dequant-to-BF16 paths.

Notably `act_quant` working is significant on its own: Triton on sm_80 cannot
represent `fp8e4nv` at all, which is what blocks the fp8 KV-cache write kernels
today (#48374). TileLang *can* do the conversion on sm_80, so the fp8 KV cache
has a viable route that does not need hand-rolled bit manipulation.

### Why it does not run today — the blocker chain

**1. No sparse-MLA attention backend admits sm_80.**

- `vllm/models/deepseek_v41/sparse_mla.py:125` — `supports_compute_capability`
  returns `capability.major in [9, 10]`
- `vllm/models/deepseek_v41/nvidia/flashinfer_sparse.py:133` —
  `capability.major in [10, 12]`

`_select_dsv4_attn_cls` (`vllm/models/deepseek_v41/nvidia/model.py:148,152`)
falls through to `DeepseekV4FlashMLAAttention` for every non-sm_12 CUDA device,
and FlashMLA's sparse kernels are SM90a/SM100f only.

**2. The plain SWA path is also FlashMLA-bound.**
`vllm/v1/attention/backends/mla/sparse_swa.py:34` imports `FlashMLASchedMeta,
get_mla_metadata` from `vllm.v1.attention.ops.flashmla` for the tile-scheduler

issues.title: [RFC]: Support ViT Full CUDA Graph (Tracker)
issues.body:
### Motivation.

Multimodal large language models (e.g., Qwen3-VL, Qwen3.5, GLM-V, Kimi K2.5) rely on a Vision Transformer (ViT) encoder to process visual inputs before feeding them into the language model backbone. In production serving scenarios, the ViT forward pass involves launching a large number of small CUDA kernels — including patch embedding, layer normalization, multi-head self-attention, and MLP projections — each of which incurs non-trivial kernel launch overhead on the host side.

Currently, vLLM supports CUDA graph capture for the decoder (LLM) portion of the model, which has proven effective at reducing kernel launch costs and improving throughput. However, the ViT encoder is still executed eagerly, meaning every forward pass re-launches all kernels from scratch. Extending full CUDA graph support to the ViT encoder would allow the entire encoder forward pass to be captured and replayed as a single graph, eliminating per-kernel launch overhead and enabling more consistent, low-latency inference for multimodal models.

issues.title: [Bug]: Wrong timestamps if audio > 30s
issues.body:
### Your current environment


NA

### 🐛 Describe the bug

**Segment level timestamps are incrementally offset by ~0.5s per segment.**

When transcribing long audio with vLLM Whisper, segment-level timestamps are increasingly inaccurate. Chunking uses by default a 1s window to find low-energy (quiet) regions for splitting, so the next chunk may start up to 1s earlier than the nominal chunk length. This offset is not compensated for when generating segment timestamps, resulting in an average delay of ~0.5s per segment, which accumulates (e.g., 5s after 10 segments).

Clients can workaround by subtracting 0.5s per segment, but that's obviously not accurate.

Also, the [related documentation](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/e83b7e379c11bf136c1b96bc6a67b6d2207cfde4/docs/contributing/model/transcription.md#audio-preprocessing-and-chunking) is not correct: there are no overlapping chunks, but just a window for searching the best split point. Maybe this confusion is the cause of the issue.

issues.title: [RFC]: Limit the use of envvars in vLLM
issues.body:
### Motivation.

vLLM's envvars are on the edge of getting out of control. There are many envvars should instead be configs. Like the attention backend, all2all kernel backend, and even there is a flag to control KV cache layout. envvars are evil because:

1. It is equivalent of using global variables everywhere in the code, which is a bad programming practice.
2. envvars have no advanced structure like, hierarchy, typechecks, etc. 

In summary, I think envvars are the kind of thing that is very easy to add so people tend to add envvars as the shortest path to implement their feature, but this can quickly becomes unmanageable and makes the project very hard to use. 

### Proposed Change.

I think we should:

1. Spend some effort on reviewing the current envvars and move many of them to configs.
2. Have very strict bar on what can be an envvar and question every new envvars in vllm.

issues.title: [Feature]: Optimize collectives in TP MoE case using torch.compile pass
issues.body:
### 🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch

To avoid redundant work in MoE models in the TP case, sequence parallelism was added to the Deepseek model definition in #24134 and expanded to other models in #24982. However, to avoid performing surgery on the linear layer, the current approach performs more communication than necessary. With a torch.compile custom pass, we can rewrite the graph to remove the redundant computation.

### More details

Before the SP optimization, the ops in the model were:
```
- o_proj:[num_tokens, ...] -> [num_tokens, ...] (incomplete results)
- all_reduce:[num_tokens, ...] -> [num_tokens, ...]
- rms_norm:[num_tokens, ...] -> [num_tokens, ...]
- router:[num_tokens, ...] -> [num_tokens, ...]
- experts:[num_tokens, ...] -> [num_tokens, ...]
- ...
```

With sequence parallel enabled, this becomes:
```
- o_proj: [num_tokens, ...] -> [num_tokens, ...] (incomplete results)
- all_reduce: [num_tokens, ...] -> [num_tokens, ...]
- rms_norm:[num_tokens, ...] -> [num_tokens, ...]
- chunk: [num_tokens, ...] -> [num_tokens/tp, ...]
- router: [num_tokens/tp, ...] -> [num_tokens/tp, ...]
- experts: [num_tokens/tp, ...] -> [num_tokens/tp, ...]
- all_gather: [num_tokens/tp, ...] -> [num_tokens, ...]
```

Additionally, experts now properly do the dp+tp<->ep dispatch instead of just the original replicated dp<->ep dispatch.

Notice that the `all_reduce` (and `rms_norm`) do redundant communication as each TP rank only requires partial results. With a compile pass, we can convert the `all_reduce` -> `rms_norm` -> `chunk` sequence into a `reduce_scatter` -> `rms_norm`:

```
- o_proj: [num_tokens, ...] -> [num_tokens, ...] (incomplete results)
- reduce_scatter: [num_tokens, ...] -> [num_tokens/tp, ...]
- router: [num_tokens/tp, ...] -> [num_tokens/tp, ...]
- experts: [num_tokens/tp, ...] -> [num_tokens/tp, ...]
- all_gather: [num_tokens/tp, ...] -> [num_tokens, ...]
```

We should create a new `SequenceParallelismMoEPass`, controlled by a new `PassConfig.enable_sp_moe` flag (following the new naming convention in #27995) so that it can be turned on independently of regular SP. We will likely need to pad the number of tokens to a multiple of TP size, although like described in #29136, there are alternatives.

#### SP
Additionally, to make SP-MoE compatible with AsyncTP, the SP pass should also replace the `all_gather` -> `rms_norm` sequence with `rms_norm` -> `all_gather`, such that the `all_gather` can be fused with the following QKV proj. We can see that in the SP case we perform an `all_gather` instead of `all_reduce` after the MLP layer.

### Alternatives

Alternatively, the original optimization could be done as a compile pass as well, which would significantly clean up the MoE model definitions. However, that would mean that `VLLM_COMPILE` compilation mode would be required for this optimization and if compilation is disabled, the optimization would be disabled as well. Generally we accept lower performance in eager mode as compilation is on by default, but I know there was a reason this was done this way (don't remember why).

We could also just let the SP pass first transform `all_reduce` -> `rms_norm` into `reduce_scatter` -> `rms_norm` -> `all_gather` and then eliminate the `all_gather` -> `chunk` combo. But then we have less control over SP after MoE (although it seems like all_reduce is not even used in that case).

### Additional context

Original proposal comment: https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/24982#pullrequest

issues.title: Upgrade to Transformers v5
issues.body:
## What is this issue?

This issue serves as a living tracker for the current issues preventing us from upgrading vLLM to Transformers v5.

We will use sub-issues to track individual failures and PRs should be made against these sub-issues.

The solutions to these issues may need to be applied to either:

- Transformers in the form of:
  - Adding missing backward compatibility (usually for custom code models)
  - General bug fixes/improvements to new features of v5
- vLLM in the form of:
  - Forward compatibility with how something is now done in v5
  - Edge case handling for issues that v4 ignored (such as config validation)

Sometimes, the issue is simply with the model checkpoint itself, for example if it:

- Contains a malformed `config.json` that cannot be used to instantiate the newly input validated `PreTrainedConfig` class
- Custom code* uses deprecated/removed APIs

In these situations, the best solution will likely be to skip these tests in vLLM and open a PR to Transformers to contribute this model. This will be faster and more sustainable than waiting for the model vendor to fix their custom model code, sometimes they nevert do.

Contributing the new model should be done using the new [Modular Transformers](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/main/en/modular_transformers) so that the implementation is easy to maintain and will remain maintained by the Transformers team.

_*particularly in the parts of the model implementation that vLLM tries to directly reuse, such as config/tokenizer/multimodal processor_

issues.title: [Feature]: `CustomOp` cleanup
issues.body:
### 🚀 Motivation

Currently, we do not have a consistent plan for "light" custom ops (subclasses of `CustomOp` with both torch-native and GPU implementations). As we work on improved performance on NVIDIA Blackwell and AMD, we should be more intentional with CompilationConfig defaults that control custom op dispatching. This is a parent issue that tracks smaller PRs addressing `CustomOp`s.

In vLLM, there are two kinds of custom kernels/ops:
1. "heavy" ops like GEMMs, MoE, and attention, which will mostly use tuned custom kernels for maximum performance.
2. "light" ops like `RMSNorm`, `SiluAndMul`, and `RoPE`, which have both torch-native and custom GPU implementations.

This issue only refers to "light" ops, which are (or should be) all subclasses of `CustomOp`.

When we enabled `torch.compile` by default in V1, the plan was to reduce our reliance on custom kernels to reduce maintenance costs and code complexity, even with minor performance costs. Recent versions of `torch` actually produce Triton kernels faster than our custom op implementations anyway.

However, with startup time concerns (#19824), it seems like we want good performance even with Inductor disabled (more discussion on startup times to come in a follow-up issue). Additionally, custom op performance has been reported to be better than torch.compile-generated Triton kernels on AMD.

### ❗ Issues

This is a list of current issues with custom ops. The following section tracks proposed and WIP solutions. Larger line items might have their own issue or get one in the future.

1. [Perf] FP8 quantization not fused with rms_norm/silu_mul (because fp8 quant doesn't have a torch native implementation)
2. [Perf] AMD uses custom ops but fusion for them is hardcoded to disabled.
3. [Perf] We don't have good visibility into performance differences between GPU and torch native implementations of custom ops across different models and hardware platforms.
4. [Perf][Code Quality] Fused and unfused custom ops currently reimplement the same code, and only some are vectorized.
5. [Testing] Custom op tests either don't exist or reimplement Torch naive implementations
6. [Compilation] Current custom passes rely on custom op pattern matching, which involves auto-functionalization (#14703) and requires custom ops to be enabled. If custom ops are slower than native impls, that means e.g. attention+quant fusion needs to take a hit on other quants to fuse the o-proj one. I'll create an RFC for this.

### ✅  Solutions

Once we have benchmarking numbers, we can set sensible defaults. Improving startup time will likely result in more explicit "profiles" with better config defaults.

Detailed solution tracking:

1. ✅ @ProExpertProg: FP8 `CustomOp`s in #19830
2. ✅ #19181 removed hardcoded `enable_fusion=False`.
3. 🚧 WIP @gshtras and @SageMoore are collecting some benchmarking numbers for custom op performance. More benchmarking can be done as needed. Automating some of this would be great as well.
4. ❗ TODO consolidating, vectorizing and cleaning up CUDA/HIP implementations of custom ops.
5. ❗ TODO add testing utilities for custom ops.
6. ✅ match and perform fusion with custom ops disabled: #24604

#### ➕ Other potential improvements

- [ ] Simplify custom op enablement
- [ ] Improve custom op documentation
- [ ] Custom op microbenchmarks

issues.title: [Docs] Document NIXL KV connector metrics aggregation semantics
issues.body:
## Summary

The NIXL KV connector logs transfer metrics periodically:

```
KV Transfer metrics: Num successful transfers=4, Avg xfer time (ms)=1.381, P90 xfer time (ms)=2.601, Avg post time (ms)=0.672, P90 post time (ms)=0.801, Avg MB per transfer=2.25, Throughput (MB/s)=1629.549, Avg number of descriptors=72.0
```

Currently there is no documentation explaining what these metrics represent, especially in the context of **multi-rank (TP > 1) deployments**. This has already caused confusion among users.

## Current behavior

All metrics are **aggregated across all TP ranks** before summary stats are computed:

1. Each TP rank independently records per-transfer telemetry (`transfer_duration`, `post_duration`, `bytes_transferred`, `num_descriptors`) via `NixlKVConnectorStats.record_transfer()` in [`stats.py`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/main/vllm/distributed/kv_transfer/kv_connector/v1/nixl/stats.py).
2. Stats from all ranks are concatenated via `aggregate()` (`list.extend()`).
3. `reduce()` computes averages, percentiles, and throughput over the **combined** pool of observations from all ranks.

This means:
- **"Num successful transfers"** is the total count across all ranks, not per-rank.
- **"Avg MB per transfer"** is the average over all individual rank-level transfers, not the total bytes moved for a single KV cache transfer operation.
- **"Throughput (MB/s)"** is `total_MB_all_ranks / total_time_all_ranks` — effectively an average per-rank throughput, not the aggregate system throughput.
- **Percentiles (P90)** are computed over the combined distribution of all ranks' transfer times.

This is unintuitive because users may expect metrics to reflect per-engine totals or aggregate system throughput.

## What needs to be documented

1. **Docstrings in `stats.py`**: Add clear documentation to `NixlKVConnectorStats` explaining that stats are aggregated across all TP ranks and what each metric represents in that context.
2. **Inline comments in `reduce()`**: Clarify the semantics of throughput and averages — that they are per-rank averages over the combined observation pool.
3. **Docstrings in `metrics.py`**: Document the `observe()` → `aggregate()` → `reduce()` → `log()` pipeline and the fact that stats arrive pre-aggregated across workers.
4. **(Optional) Docs page**: Add a section to the disaggregated serving documentation explaining how to interpret the KV Transfer metrics log line.

## Relevant files

- `vllm/distributed/kv_transfer/kv_connector/v1/nixl/stats.py` — `NixlKVConnectorStats` (recording, aggregation, reduction)
- `vllm/distributed/kv_transfer/kv_connector/v1/metrics.py` — `KVConnectorLogging` (observe/log pipeline), `KVConnectorStats` (base class)

## Context

See related discussion: metrics are aggregated across ranks rather than reported per-rank or per-engine. This is a deliberate design choice (fire-and-forget from workers), but it needs to be clearly documented so users can correctly interpret the numbers.

issues.title: [Transformers v5] InternVL2
issues.body:
This is a sub-issue forming part of the work in https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/38379, please read the description of this issue before beginning to work on this one.

## Which test is failing?

Transformers v5 creates the model on the meta device first, then loads the weights, similarly to what vLLM does. The issue here is that the custom model code in the checkpoint tries to use real tensors as part of model structure construction.

Since the issue here is with the HF reference generation, this cannot be fixed in vLLM (other than skipping the tests until the model works with Transformers v5). The proper solution to this issue is to upstream this architecture, which shouldn't be too hard using Modular Transformers as the text backbone is Qwen2 so that can be reused.

```console
$ pytest tests/models/multimodal/generation/test_common.py::test_single_image_models[intern_vl-test_case25]
...
RuntimeError: Tensor.item() cannot be called on meta tensors
```

## How to configure my environment?

It's very important that you install both vLLM and Transformers from source so that your test results reflect the current state of both libraries.

```console
# Or your fork
git clone https://github.com/huggingface/transformers.git
git clone https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm.git

cd vllm
VLLM_USE_PRECOMPILED=1 uv pip install -e .
uv pip install -e ../transformers
```

issues.title: [Bug]: ModelOpt Llama-4 Checkpoints Take 5+ minutes to load
issues.body:
### 🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch

In working on some MoE refactors, I discovered that L4 for ModelOpt takes 5+minutes to load weights even from CPU page cache. 
- https://huggingface.co/nvidia/Llama-4-Scout-17B-16E-Instruct-FP8

The root cause is basically this hack logic to load the state dict that ModelOpt uses
- https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/main/vllm/model_executor/models/llama4.py#L439-L523 [modelopt is the fused case] 

What happens is that the CPU tensor (loaded weight) that we are going to load into the GPU tensor (param) becomes non-contiguous due to this logic. As a result, when we eventually call `_copy()` from CPU->GPU we are calling this on a non-contiguous cpu tensor which takes 3-4s per weight.

To hack around this for local R&D, I simply immediately move the loaded_weight to the GPU. This makes the gather happen on the GPU which accelerates things a lot. This isn't reasonable as an actual solution though

We should investigate where the logic in the weight loader can avoid creating non-contiguous CPU tensors
